name: Marco Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a transmission crew, the big steel towers that carry power across the hills from the hydro dam down to the cities. We work two weeks on, one week off, living in a work camp out past Copper Ridge. I'm a helper, so I'm on the ground: bolting tower sections together, running the winch, fetching and carrying, keeping out of the way of the people who know more than me. The day starts at six with the safety talk and ends when the light goes. I like the quiet and the views; I don't like the bunkhouse snoring or being away from Rosa.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing this?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two and a half years. Before that I was a fitter at the copper mine for thirty-one years, until it shut in 2023. Nothing else in Copper Ridge pays, so when the power company came through hiring helpers for the new line, I took it. Lower pay than the mine, but it's a wage, and at my age you take the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then. I don't go online much, and at camp nobody talks about AI anyway; it's football and the weather. If someone asked, I'd say I never thought it would come out here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means nothing for me. I'm on a tower in the hills, and no computer is bolting those sections together. I'd keep doing what I'm doing until they tell me to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, same as now. Two weeks on, one week off, send the money home, keep the truck running. If there's overtime on the next tower job, I'd take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. Nothing changes, and I'm used to nothing changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're used to nothing changing. But your mine closed. How does that fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. The mine closing wasn't a computer, it was copper prices and a company far away. Things change, sure, but not usually because of gadgets. I suppose I'd still be waiting for the next price drop or the next company decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does money look like week to week right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. Rosa does hair from the front room, a few clients a week, and that covers the food. My wage covers the mortgage, the truck and the power bill, and after that there's maybe enough for one dinner out a month. We had some savings from the mine payout, but that went on the roof and our daughter's wedding.

S0.say: That's that, then. He doesn't go online, nobody at camp talks about AI, and he never thought it would reach out where he works.
S0.think: It means nothing for him, because no computer is bolting tower sections together in the hills. He would keep working until told to stop.
S0.do: Keeps working two weeks on, one week off, sending money home and keeping the truck running. Takes any overtime on the next tower job.
S0.feel: Calm, used to things not changing.
S0.quote: The mine closing wasn't a computer, it was copper prices and a company far away.
S0.fieldNote: Marco is quiet and matter-of-fact, with a fitter's practical way of seeing things. He sees change as coming from prices and distant companies rather than technology. His mine payout already went on a roof and a wedding, which explains the thin savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. At camp I'd probably say they'll never get a robot up a tower in this wind. I wouldn't say much online, because I'm not on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think the office people go first, the planners and the ones who do the schedules. Out here, maybe they'd bring in drones to check the lines instead of us walking them. I'd hope it stays like that till I'm done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, at first. I'd wait and see what the company actually does before I change anything. If the overtime started drying up, I'd cut back, maybe stop the dinners out and put off fixing the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not panicking, but I'd keep my ears open at the camp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would make you stop waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they cut a crew, or if the foreman started saying we're on short contracts. That's what happened at the mine first: short contracts, then fewer shifts, then the letter. I'd know the signs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course, if the company offered one on the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'm not a computer man, never have been. If they made me, I'd go, but I'd sit at the back and hope it was short.

S1.say: We'll see. At camp he'd joke that they'll never get a robot up a tower in this wind.
S1.think: He expects office planners to go first, with drones perhaps replacing line patrols out in the field. He hopes the ground work lasts until he's done.
S1.do: Waits to see what the company does before changing anything. Cuts dinners out and puts off truck repairs if overtime dries up, and avoids training courses unless required.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, keeping his ears open at camp.
S1.quote: That's what happened at the mine first: short contracts, then fewer shifts, then the letter.
S1.fieldNote: Marco reads the situation through his mine closure, watching for the same warning signs. He is open about not wanting to learn new technology. His default is to wait and react rather than prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not right, and someone should have thought it through. I'm not one for protests, but I'd say it at camp. I'd want the government to do something sensible, not just argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and I'm sixty. If robots can put up towers by 2028, I've got nothing. No savings, no other jobs in Copper Ridge, no skills that a robot can't do better. I'd be finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, cut everything: no dinners out, sell the truck and buy something cheap. Ask about government support, even though I've never asked for anything. Rosa would have to take on more clients, and maybe our son in the city could help a bit with the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's gone. I'd be lying awake every night in the bunkhouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of that picture, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Telling Rosa. When the mine closed, I came home and sat in the truck for twenty minutes before I could go in. I don't think I could do that twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do with the two years of warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'm not good at planning ahead, never have been. Maybe sell the camper, put that money aside, but that's maybe three thousand, and that doesn't last long.

S2.say: It's not right, and someone should have thought it through. He is not one for protests but would want the government to do something sensible.
S2.think: At sixty with no savings and no other jobs in town, robots putting up towers would leave him with nothing. He would feel finished.
S2.do: Cuts everything, sells the truck for something cheaper and the camper for about three thousand. Asks about government support for the first time, and leans on his partner Rosa and his son.
S2.feel: Like the ground has gone, lying awake every night.
S2.quote: When the mine closed, I came home and sat in the truck for twenty minutes before I could go in.
S2.fieldNote: Marco has no plan for the fast scenario and says so plainly. Telling Rosa, not the job loss itself, is what he dreads most. He is willing to accept government help, though he has never asked before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit better, but not much. At camp I'd say we've got time to sort ourselves out. I'd still want the government to sort out something for older workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to sixty-three. That's close to the pension, so maybe I could hang on. I'd still be scared about money, but there's at least a chance of getting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save a bit each month, maybe a hundred, even if it means no dinners out. I'd look at whether I could retire at sixty-three on a reduced pension. And I'd keep working as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not as bad. There's a bit of light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A hundred a month. Where would that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dinners out, the beer at camp, and I'd stop smoking, which Rosa's been on at me about for years. That's probably a hundred and fifty right there. Funny how the money's always there when you're scared enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would early retirement on a reduced pension look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small. We'd sell the house, maybe, and buy something smaller in town. Rosa keeps doing hair, I'd do odd jobs, fix things for neighbours. We'd manage, I think, if the roof holds.

S3.say: Five years is a bit better but not much. He would tell his crew there's time to sort things out and still want the government to help older workers.
S3.think: At sixty-three he would be close to his pension, so he might hang on. He is still scared about money but sees a chance.
S3.do: Saves about a hundred a month by cutting dinners out and beer and quitting smoking. Looks into retiring at sixty-three on a reduced pension and keeps working as long as he's wanted.
S3.feel: Worried, but with a bit of light.
S3.quote: Funny how the money's always there when you're scared enough.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Marco a reason to start saving, though only through cuts he has resisted for years. Early retirement on a reduced pension is his realistic exit. He still loses sleep because the margin is so thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll be out of it by then. At camp I'd say good luck to the young ones. Nothing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years takes me to sixty-eight, so I'd be retired. The worry is whether the pension's enough, because it's small. But the job itself would see me out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep working, put a bit away if I can. I'd tell our son to think about his job driving buses, because that might be gone by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, about the pension and the kids. For me it's almost all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son about his bus job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep your eyes open, and don't wait for the letter like I did. He'd probably say, Dad, you're worrying too much. Maybe I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's almost all right for you. What's the 'almost'?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pension, and Rosa. She's younger than me by four years, so she'd still be working when the robots come in, and doing hair might not be safe either. I'd worry about her more than me.

S4.say: He'll be out of it by then, before the machines arrive. At camp he'd wish the young ones good luck and say nothing online.
S4.think: At sixty-eight he would be retired, with the job seeing him out. His worry is whether his small pension will be enough.
S4.do: Keeps working and puts a little away when possible. Tells his son to think about whether his bus-driving job will last.
S4.feel: Uneasy about his pension and his family, but almost all right for himself.
S4.quote: She's younger than me by four years, so she'd still be working when the robots come in, and doing hair might not be safe either.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Marco see his way to retirement, so his worry shifts to his small pension, his son and his wife Rosa. He stays quiet and understated. His advice to his son echoes his own regret about waiting at the mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd have no time and nothing to fall back on. What would help is something that gets people my age to the pension, a bridge or a payout. I'm not going to learn computers at sixty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe you should've asked about places like Copper Ridge, where there's only one or two employers. When one goes, you can't just walk down the road and get another job. Out here, the power company is the only wage left in town, and I'm holding onto it with both hands.

headlineQuote: Out here, the power company is the only wage left in town, and I'm holding onto it with both hands.
portrait: Marco Ito is a 58-year-old helper on a transmission tower crew, working two weeks on and one off from a camp near Copper Ridge, after thirty-one years as a fitter at a copper mine that closed in 2023. He and his wife Rosa, who does hair from their front room, have almost no savings since the mine payout went on a roof and a wedding. He never uses AI and prefers to wait and see before changing anything. In the milder pictures he hopes the remote tower work outlasts him; in the 2028 picture he feels finished. With five or ten years he looks for a path to the pension and worries for his son and Rosa.
biggestWorry: The 2028 scenario, because he would have no time and nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge or payout that gets people his age to the pension, because he won't learn computers at sixty.
